1.0.0.en: Ramathaim-Zophim: this is the city of Ramah, which lies about ten miles north of Jerusalem. It was the home of Samuel's family, and it was also the city from which Joseph of Arimathea came in the days of Christ. The word Zophim refers to Samuel's fourth forefather, who may have been the first of the family to dwell in this city. There are several cities called Ramah, so the text distinguishes this one by saying Ramathaim-Zophim.

1.0.1.en: The book begins by introducing to us the person of Samuel's father. It tells us his name, "Elkanah," and his home, the city of Ramah, and it also lists his ancestors back to the great-grandfather, to confirm his identity and his belonging to the tribe of Levi (the Kohathites), who are mentioned in more detail in (1 Chr 6:20-27). The word Ephraimite means that he dwelt in the midst of the tribe of Ephraim, for he lived in the hill country of Ephraim.

1.1.0.en: Elkanah had two wives, since the Jewish law permitted polygamy. The first was Hannah, the mother of Samuel, who was barren and without offspring, and the other was named Peninnah, and she had children.

1.2.0.en: Shiloh: a city lying north of Bethel and 17 miles north of Jerusalem. Joshua moved the tabernacle of meeting there from Gilgal, and the tabernacle remained there for about 310 years. Eli the priest and Samuel dwelt there.

1.2.1.en: As an indication of the piety of Elkanah, the husband and father, we learn that he was religious and constant in worship, and did not neglect to go up to the house of the Lord every year to offer sacrifices for himself, his children and his wives, according to the commandment of the Lord. The Law commanded going to the house of the Lord three times a year, at the feasts of Passover, Harvest and Tabernacles. In that period they had neglected to keep the three feasts, and they used to go only at the Feast of Harvest, as Jewish tradition declares. The house of the Lord at that time was the tabernacle of meeting, which had been set up in the city of "Shiloh." This verse also tells us that Eli was the high priest at that time, and that he had two sons who were priests, "Hophni" and "Phinehas."

1.3.0.en: Some sacrifices, such as the peace offering, were divided between God, whose portion was burned on the altar, and the priests, who had the front leg and part of the breast. As for most of the sacrifice, it was eaten by the one who offered it, together with the Levites and the poor.

1.3.1.en: When Elkanah gave portions to his wife Peninnah and her children, he did not wrong them; but he favored Hannah with a double portion. The inspired text makes clear to us the reason for this: that her husband loved her more than Peninnah, who had the children, and perhaps also as a compensation for her and a comfort to her heart for not bearing children because her womb was closed. Elkanah's love for Hannah troubled Peninnah, so she provoked Hannah, as appears from (v. 6). The First Book of Samuel. And Peninnah, with her many children, is a type of the Jewish nation, which had a portion with God, while Hannah is a type of the Church of the Gentiles, which was barren before she enjoyed her heavenly Bridegroom, "Christ," and then became possessed of a blessed offspring greater than that of the first.

1.3.2.en: Take care to compensate every weak person around you with your tenderness, and encourage him so that he may continue his life with contentment and joy, as Elkanah did with barren Hannah, but with wisdom, so that you do not trouble others.

1.4.1.en: Perhaps because of Elkanah's evident love for his wife Hannah, or because he gave her two portions, "Peninnah" felt jealous, and she kept vexing Hannah with the wounding words of women, taunting her and boasting over her that she was the one with offspring and children, and that the Lord had deprived Hannah of children and motherhood.

1.4.2.en: This action of "Peninnah" was repeated whenever she went up with her husband and Hannah to the house of the Lord. Consequently the days of the feast and of the joy of offering sacrifices were nothing more than days of sorrow for Hannah, who expressed her sorrow, when it became more than she could bear, by refraining from eating of the sacrifices and from taking part in the celebration of the feast.

1.5.0.en: Elkanah, the loving husband, sensed the oppression and sorrow that his wife was suffering, so he wanted to relieve her and comfort her heart with gentle words. He told her that, since he loved her and she felt it, was this not enough, and better than her having ten sons?

1.5.1.en: May you feel for those around you and sympathize with their problems, and try to help them as far as you are able, and offer them kind words that lift their sorrows from them, for in this you offer love to Christ Himself.

1.6.0.en: A post of the temple of the Lord: beside the door of the temple.

1.6.1.en: Hannah responded to her husband's kind words and ate with them of the sacrifices, but her heart was still sorrowful and her wound deep. So she went with all her distress, "bitter in soul," to the house of the Lord. "Eli" the high priest was sitting beside its door, and as soon as Hannah arrived she began to pray in sorrow, overcome by her burning tears.

1.7.0.en: No razor shall come upon his head: one of the features of the law of the vow was that a person was not to cut his hair throughout the period of his vow.

1.7.1.en: In Hannah's fervent prayer she made a vow to God: that if He would remove her humiliation and give her a son, she would give him to the Lord as a servant and a Nazirite in His house all the days of his life.

1.8.0.en: Hannah prayed a long, deep and moving prayer. No one heard her voice, but Eli the priest watched the movements of her lips and thought she was drunk, since he was not accustomed to seeing such a sight in contrite prayer before God.

1.9.0.en: Eli the priest spoke, rebuking her and disapproving of her state: how could she stand without propriety before the Lord in His house, in a state of drunkenness and immodesty unbecoming to the holiness of the house of God? For her head was moving, and so were her lips, as if she were reeling and shaking from wine, like one who cannot stand with composure and reverence, so he supposed she had drunk much wine.

1.9.1.en: Eli thought this because, sadly, when they ate of the peace offerings they would drink wine to the point of drunkenness, and this shows the degree of spiritual decline to which they had come at that time.

1.10.0.en: Belial: the name of a well-known pagan god, and it is a symbol of Satan.

1.10.1.en: In humility Hannah defended herself, explaining that she was not drunk but broken-hearted and sorrowful, and that she was pouring herself out in contrition before the Lord. She denied that she was a worshipper of Satan or one who despised the house of God, and said that it was her concern and grief that had driven her to speak with God in this manner and for this length of time.

1.10.2.en: This shows her good manners and humility, for she did not reply to Eli that he was unable to tell fervent prayer from drunkenness, and she did not condemn him for his indulgence toward his sons the priests, who filled the temple with evil by falling into adultery and theft, as will appear in the following verses.

1.11.0.en: Eli the priest changed his attitude after he heard Hannah's words and her defense and understood her situation, so he prayed for her peace, and that God, the Maker of good things, would give her all that she had asked of Him in her prayer ...

1.12.0.en: Let your maidservant find grace in your sight: an expression meaning "may you be pleased with me and bless me."

1.12.1.en: Before Hannah went away, with the utmost courtesy and humility, she asked for the priest's blessing. Having set her problem before the Lord and spoken with the priest, she went back in a different state, for she went to eat, and her face was no longer sad as it had been.

1.12.2.en: From all that has gone before we learn some useful spiritual lessons, among them:

1.12.3.en: 1- Hannah was a spiritual woman, yet subject to human weakness, and when she could not overcome her anxiety she turned to God and to His house to pour out what was in her heart.

1.12.4.en: 2- Her prayer was long, deep and persistent, and she did not care whether any person heard what she said, but sought God alone.

1.12.5.en: 3- Hannah was a humble woman, and she addressed the priest with these humble expressions: "your handmaid," "your maidservant," "let me find grace in your sight."

1.12.6.en: 4- Eli the priest was also zealous for the house of God, for when he suspected that Hannah was drunk, he did not hesitate to rebuke her. A priest must be moved by a holy zeal for the house of God.

1.12.7.en: 5- How sweet is the word "Go in peace," which the Lord of glory Himself used, and which the priests now use in the Church at the end of dismissing the people, when the last words are "Go in peace ... the peace of the Lord be with you all."

1.13.s.en: (3) The birth of Samuel and his presentation to the Lord

1.13.0.en: At the end of their visit to the temple and their offering of sacrifices, they worshipped the Lord before returning to their town. On their return the inspired text mentions the words "the Lord remembered her," which means that the Lord answered her prayer and the priest's blessing upon her. So Hannah conceived within the same year and bore a male son, and called his name Samuel. The meaning of his name is "asked of God" or "the name of God."

1.14.0.en: The Lord establish His word: God fulfills His promise of accepting Samuel as a Nazirite, as Hannah said in her prayer (v. 11). Elkanah the man and his household went up the following year to offer his sacrifices to God as usual, but Hannah excused herself from going with him until Samuel was weaned, so that there would be one visit in which she would present her son as a Nazirite to God, for she did not wish to go and return without presenting him to the Lord. Her husband "Elkanah" agreed with her opinion that the visit should be postponed until the child Samuel was weaned, and he prayed to God to fulfill His promise of accepting the child as a Nazirite to Him. Here appear Hannah's piety and her great love for God: although this was her only son, she gave him to God to serve in His temple. Her love for God overcame her love for her son, that is, she gave up her motherhood for the sake of God.

1.15.0.en: When she had weaned him: the period of nursing children in those days was about two years.

1.15.1.en: A skin of wine: a leather vessel like a waterskin, used for carrying liquids.

1.15.2.en: An ephah of flour: a measure of flour equal to 22.9 liters.

1.15.3.en: After the little boy Samuel was weaned, Hannah went with her son, and of course her husband, to the tabernacle of meeting at "Shiloh" to fulfill her vow. She took with her three bulls to offer, perhaps to offer them as a "burnt offering," a "sin offering" and a "peace offering" for the boy. She also brought the wine that is poured out on the sacrifices as the Law prescribes, and the flour that is offered as an offering to God (Lev 1, 3, 4). The inspired text mentions that Hannah brought her son up, and not she and Elkanah, to confirm that it was she who thought of presenting her son as a Nazirite to God, and Elkanah agreed to it.

1.15.4.en: Hannah fulfilled her vow and gave her only son to God. May you be generous in your giving, and give to God the dearest thing you have and the best of what you possess, not only material things, but if your son wishes to consecrate his life to God, may you encourage him and not think selfishly of keeping him for yourself.

1.16.0.en: As your soul lives: an expression meaning "may God give you life."

1.16.1.en: Hannah stood before "Eli" the priest and spoke in a courteous manner, saying "I ask you, my lord," to request his permission to be heard, and she reminded him that she was the same woman who had stood before him some time before to pray to the Lord that He would give her a boy. She pointed to Samuel, the subject of the conversation, and went on to say that the Lord had accomplished His work and given her what she had asked of Him.

1.17.0.en: I have lent him to the Lord: I have presented him to the Lord.

1.17.1.en: Lent: a loan or an advance.

1.17.2.en: Hannah acknowledges God's favor toward her and that He gave her the petition of her heart, and she is here today to present her son to God. Although God gave her a son who belongs to her by physical sonship, and she became also a mother to him, "the mother of Samuel," she lends him as a permanent loan to the Lord, that is, she gave what was hers to the Lord. The expression "as long as he lives" means that she would no longer wish for him or long for him for herself, or regret his separation from her, but she made her son Samuel worship before the house of God. Perhaps in his childhood he did not fully understand what he was doing, but the meaning is very beautiful, that the consecrated one begins by offering his life to the Lord by worshipping Him, as a clear expression of complete submission to His will and purpose.

1.17.3.en: The First Book of Samuel. The song of Hannah and the sin of Eli's sons

2.0.0.en: My horn: an expression of Hannah's strength, for she borrowed for it the horn of the animal, which represents its strength.

2.0.1.en: My mouth is enlarged: I have become able to answer those who taunted me.

2.0.2.en: In joy after sorrow and brokenness, Hannah stood before God repeating her prayer, her praise and her glorification of the Lord for His gift to her. She began her prayer by declaring this joy, and that it was joy in the Lord's work with her more than joy in her son himself. For He had restored her honor after her brokenness and lifted up her head before those who taunted her, and she regarded what God had done with her as deliverance from her shame and disgrace. The expression "I rejoice in Your salvation" also reminds us of the song of the Holy Virgin, "My spirit rejoices in God my Savior" (Lk 1:46). Here appears Hannah's concern to give thanks to God, which many neglect after their troubles are relieved. And although Hannah had prayed in silence during her bitterness (ch. 1), when she gave thanks her voice rose to glorify God. The reason for this thanksgiving is the glorification of God, not the vexing of her enemies. The deliverance of the children of Israel from their enemies the Philistines was accomplished afterward by the hand of Samuel (ch. 7:8-13), and then in the fullness of time Christ triumphed over Satan and bound him by the Cross.

2.1.0.en: There is none like You, O God, in Your holiness, and no one is able to draw near to it, for there is none like You, and there is no one in Your power, for You are like the rock on which man leans.

2.2.0.en: "Hannah" addresses the wicked and rebukes them for their pride and arrogance in their speech, and calls them to leave their insolent and mocking talk, because God knows what they think and conceal in their hearts. The expression "by Him actions are weighed" corresponds to "He repays each one according to his work."

2.3.0.en: The bows of the mighty: the bows of the mighty men.

2.3.1.en: Were girded with strength: they put on power and courage.

2.3.2.en: "Hannah" continues describing the works of God. She describes Him as the One who breaks the might of the proud and everything on which they rely, like the weapons of war that the bows symbolize, while the weak and humble He gave strength, victory and courage.

2.4.0.en: Likewise everyone who boasted of possessing the means of life and luxury .. their condition reached the point that they became poor, so that they worked as hired men and slaves to find the bread they would eat, while the hungry, who have no one but God, have been filled to satisfaction. And the barren one (meaning Hannah) has seven children, a figure of speech for the abundance of her offspring, while she who had many children (Peninnah) has withered, and the glory of her boasting has passed away, because the reason for her boasting was evil, namely the vexing of others.

2.4.1.en: The First Book of Samuel. The barren woman (Hannah) is a type of the Gentiles who became Christians and whose number has become great, while the Jews who rejected Christ, whom Peninnah signifies, have become weak. The number seven signifies perfection, that is, God gave Hannah sufficient offspring, although she actually bore three sons and two daughters (v. 21).

2.5.0.en: God alone has the authority to put to death whom He wills and to save whom He wills, and He also makes poor whom He wills and makes rich whom He wills; He brings the proud down and lifts the humble up..; and this is also like the song of the Virgin when she said, "He has put down the mighty from their thrones, and exalted the lowly" (Lk 1:52).

2.6.0.en: The pillars of the earth: an expression that God is the Creator and Founder of the earth, like one who raises a building on pillars.

2.6.1.en: "Hannah" continues glorifying the Lord in His works. She points to Him in His raising the poor man trodden by people in the dust of the earth, and the needy man despised in the eyes of people, to give them honor and glory, so that their seat is among the nobles, that is, they become among the great, because God is the Founder of the earth, who established it and created it, and He possesses everything on it, and He is the Molder of the creation of people, so He is able to do all things.

2.7.0.en: God is the Keeper of those who fear Him, and He steadies their feet before hardships, while the wicked end in shame and the darkness of hell. Who then thinks that man's strength is from himself? No one is overcome or victorious unless God is his support and his hope.

2.8.0.en: Continuing the same meaning: whoever opposes God and is hostile to Him is broken, and God declares His wrath against him from heaven, for He alone is the just Judge of all the earth, and He is the Giver of honor, glory and blessing to those whom He chose of His anointed kings.

2.8.1.en: It is not hidden from the dear reader that these words are prophetic of Christ, God incarnate. His enemies have been humbled, while glory, honor and power are the attributes inseparable from the glory and divinity of the Son.

2.9.0.en: This verse refers to Elkanah's return with his family to his dwelling place at Ramah after leaving Samuel in the care of Eli the high priest, so that he might teach him how to serve the house of the Lord.

2.9.1.en: Let us also learn to plant our children in the Church from their youth to learn the hymns and the melodies, and at the suitable age to present them to receive the blessing of service as deacons, so that they may grow up in this beautiful spiritual and ecclesiastical atmosphere, and this will be reflected on their whole life afterward with blessing and spirituality.

2.10.0.en: Belial: a Hebrew word meaning without profit, and it was afterward applied to Satan.

2.10.1.en: Fleshhook: a long fork used in cooking, not like the familiar eating fork.

2.10.2.en: Laver: a basin containing water, used here to wash the slaughtered meat.

2.10.3.en: The cauldron: a large copper vessel for boiling water.

2.10.4.en: Eli the high priest had two sons who were priests, but they turned aside into many evils until they became like sons of Satan. They abandoned the law of God, and were not content with the priests' due from the sacrifices. Rather, when the people offered the sacrifices and ate them in the holy place, that is, beside the tabernacle of meeting, a representative of the two would come by with a fleshhook in his hand The First Book of Samuel and thrust it into the pot of meat, and of course he would choose the best piece, and if anyone objected he would tell him with authority that this was for the priests, and he would be silent for fear of their authority. Thus they fell into the sin of theft by compulsion.

2.11.0.en: The Law required that the Lord's portion be offered first, before any other portions, and this portion, from the fat, the liver and the two kidneys, was burned on the altar, while the priests' portion was the breast and the right leg (Lev 3:3-5). The priests and the people knew this well, but because of the greed of the priests, the sons of Eli, they were brazenly asking the people to take from the sacrifices before God's portion was offered. And although the simple people warned them not to break the Law, they were thieves, and they took a portion for themselves before God, and if the one offering the sacrifice did not allow this, they took by force what they wanted ... and this is what is now called thuggery.

2.12.0.en: The young men: what is meant is the sons of Eli the priest.

2.12.1.en: As a result of the evils of the representatives of Eli's sons in seizing the people's rights, the people were made to stumble by the priests, and they lost their reverence for the temple and its worship and despised the Law.

2.12.2.en: ?No person, however great, is above sin. Here we have priests who are supposed to be the example for the people, yet they sank to the worst level, and this teaches us fear and caution. Let us not rely on the righteousness of our fathers or trust in ourselves, but let us examine all our conduct carefully, especially what concerns God's rights and our duties toward Him, so that we do not fall into contempt and anger God!?!

2.13.s.en: (3) The service of Samuel and God's blessing on Hannah

2.13.0.en: Ephod: a linen garment like a vest, with two bands like a belt with which it is tied around a person's waist. The ephod was among the garments of the Levites and was sometimes worn by the priests. The child and boy Samuel began his service in the house of the Lord, and because of his piety and Eli the priest's love for him, Eli clothed him with an ephod as a mark distinguishing him, despite his young age. His mother kept visiting him as usual every year, and out of her care for her son, whom she had not forgotten, the inspired text tells us that she made him a robe of wool (a tunic) for the boy to wear under the ephod in the days of winter.

2.13.1.en: Hannah's care for raising her son and instructing him in the spiritual teachings is evident, for she kept him in purity despite the evils of the priests in the temple.

2.14.0.en: Lent: she lent to the Lord and presented her son to Him (see ch. 1:28). Eli admired the piety of Samuel and his parents, especially Hannah, and blessed them from God, and prophesied to Hannah that she would bear sons in place of Samuel whom she had vowed to God. After receiving the blessing, they left Shiloh and returned to their town Ramah.

2.15.1.en: The years passed and God's promise was fulfilled, and Hannah bore three sons and two daughters, and during these years Samuel was growing in piety before God in His house.

2.15.2.en: Blessed is he who offers his life or his children to God with a willing heart. Did not the Lord Christ promise him a hundredfold..? God never remains in debt to His children, for in His fatherhood He accepts their gifts, and in His fatherhood He also grants them abundant gifts and reward.

2.16.0.en: Eli was very advanced in years, and the people reported to him all that his sons the priests were doing of plundering, looting and seizing the Lord's portions of the sacrifices. Indeed they fell into adultery with the women who assembled at the door of the tabernacle of meeting as volunteers to help in the service (such as washing the sacrifices and cleaning them) before the house of the Lord.

2.17.0.en: Eli rebuked his two sons for the evils they were doing, and told them that their deeds were not right and caused the people to stumble, since they became an evil example and the people fell into many sins. We notice here Eli's weakness, for he did not rebuke them sternly, nor did he take any action against them, such as preventing them from serving, even temporarily, although they ought to have been put to death, or at least removed completely from the service, according to what the Law commands. This angered God, so He allowed their death, and their father's, in the battle against the Philistines (ch. 4).

2.18.0.en: If a person sins against another and does not repent and make amends, God judges him; how much more, then, if a person sins directly against God, he deserves a great punishment. This is what the sons of Eli did, so God allowed them to die because of their evil in the battle against the Philistines.

2.19.0.en: This verse comes as a parenthesis in the context of the account of Eli and his sons. After the review of the evil that had penetrated the souls of the priests, we see a bright picture of the young lad Samuel, who is noted as growing in his love for God, and how God also gave him favor in the eyes of the people, who saw his goodness in the midst of all this evil.

2.19.1.en: Do not seek an excuse for yourself and fall into sin because of the spread of evil around you. Here is Samuel living in piety in the midst of the evil atmosphere. Indeed God allows your presence among the wicked so that you may be a light to the world, and be confident that He will help you to live in righteousness, whatever the pressures surrounding you.

2.20.0.en: A man of God: an expression used for the prophets or prominent spiritual figures such as "Elijah and Elisha."

2.20.1.en: God did not address Eli directly for his great fault in being lax with his sons, but sent him a prophet (whose name is unknown) as a final warning to him to repent before the punishment came upon him. He told him a message, the beginning of which The First Book of Samuel was: "Did I not reveal Myself to your fathers and forefathers (Moses and Aaron) during the humiliation of My people in the land of Egypt in the bondage of Pharaoh.

2.21.0.en: And I chose the house of Aaron, that is, your fathers, to be priests to Me and to stand before the altar to offer incense to My holy name morning and evening, and I gave them to wear the ephod and all the garments of the priesthood, and I made them heads over the people who accept their sacrifices, and guides to Israel's civil leaders when they come to seek My voice and My counsel through them.

2.22.0.en: God showed Eli that He had honored him and glorified him with the priesthood, but he despised the holiness of the house of the Lord and its worship, and honored his sons at God's expense. He left them to do evil and was content with reproof, and did not prevent their evils.

2.23.0.en: God honored the house of Eli with the priesthood as long as they held fast to His Law, but if they despised God and did not honor Him, God would punish them and humble them.

2.24.0.en: God mentions a second punishment, which is "cutting off the arm." The arm is a figure for strength and for the time of a man's youth, so the punishment is that God will destroy Eli's offspring of priests in their youth, and none of them will remain to old age. Long life in the Old Testament was one of the signs of God's blessing on a person.

2.25.0.en: Likewise, among the punishments that will come upon "Eli" is that he will see hard days for the house of the Lord, which will be assaulted in his days by the Philistines, who will take the "ark of the covenant" with them to their land. With the disappearance of the ark all the glory of Israel also disappears, and their sense of the presence of their God among them, so the feasts, the sacrifices and the joys disappear, all of which God had ordained as a kindness to His people and for the joy of their hearts.

2.26.0.en: Among the punishments also coming upon "Eli the priest" is that God will leave some of his offspring as priests serving the altar, but they will be a cause of pain to his soul and weeping to his eyes, because of the evil of their deeds on the one hand, and on the other because of their suffering from afflictions and poverty and their loss of God's blessing and grace in their lives. God also confirms, as He said before, that they will not live long but will die in their youth.

2.27.0.en: The sign He leaves for him to confirm the truth of His words is that he will hear of the death of his two sons the priests "Hophni and Phinehas" in one day.

2.27.1.en: We notice that Eli received great honor as high priest, but he did not bear the responsibility of his position; rather he was lax with his sons, so he received a severe divine punishment. As for Samuel, whom the people rejected as the voice of God and asked for a king for themselves, he endured, and then God honored him and he became one of the greatest prophets.

2.28.0.en: This verse can be interpreted directly: that this is what actually happened when God chose Samuel as His priest to offer sacrifices for the people, although he was not of the offspring of Aaron the priest but of the ordinary Levites, but God alone has the authority. Samuel was indeed faithful and zealous for God and His house, obedient and carrying out His will; and the expression "I will build him a sure house" means that the priesthood will be in his house and to his offspring after him, and he will be a leader of the people and a guide to the anointed king afterward to rule the people.

2.28.1.en: As for the prophetic meaning of this verse, it was fulfilled perfectly in the person of the Lord Jesus, who has the permanent, eternal priesthood, and whose new house became His Church, and who also became its King, its Guide and its Governor to perfection.

2.29.0.en: Continuing the discussion of the punishment, everyone who remains alive of the descendants of "Eli the priest" comes to the new priest established according to God's heart, who is Samuel, in humiliation and brokenness to ask for some money or even a piece of bread, and begs him to find a place and a portion in the service of the priesthood so that he may be able to live.

2.29.1.en: My God and my Lord ... how my heart trembled and my knees shook as I read these severe and just punishments for the one who was lax with Your rights. I beg You, my God, never allow me to neglect Your commands and Your commandments, but make me always watchful and attentive ... and have mercy on me according to Your great mercy.
